newsitem.title: FRANCE: NETHERLANDS - EXTRACTS FROM OECD ECONOMIC OUTLOOK.
newsitem.headline: NETHERLANDS - EXTRACTS FROM OECD ECONOMIC OUTLOOK.

text.p: The following extracts are taken from the Netherlands section of the June 1997 Economic Outlook published by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD):
"Real GDP growth is projected to increase, from 2.7 percent in 1996 to three percent in 1997 and 3.15 in 1998, with net exports progressively taking over as the driving force."
"With output rising above potential, and due to the recent depreciation of the guilder in effective terms, some upward pressure on wages and prices is likely to emerge."

"Real GDP growth, which reached three percent in the final quarter of 1996 and 2.7 percent for the year as a whole, seems to be continuing at a robust pace. Despite lower growth in disposable income, the driving force of expansion has been private consumption, which has been boosted by rising confidence."

"Economic growth in the Netherlands has typically followed conjunctural developments in Germany closely. Over the past few years however, there has been a pronounced decoupling, with the Netherlands performing significantly better than Germany and its neighbouring countries in general. The Dutch economy is apparently benefiting from several years of wage moderation combined with structural reforms in the labour market and the social security system, as well as deregulation in product markets..."

"Although the saving ratio is projected to decline further this year, the growth of disposable in come in 1997-98 is unlikely to be sufficiently rapid to maintain the current buoyancy of private consumption. On the other hand, the depreciation of the guilder in effective terms and the projected upturn in continental Europe should boost exports which can thus be expected to take over as the driving force of expansion."
"Short-term (interest) rates may remain around current levels, while long-term rates may edge up in 1998 in line with German rates."

"Real GDP is projected to accelerate to three percent in 1997 and 3.25 percent in 1998, reflecting a stong pick-up in exports. The contribution of the foreign balance to growth is expected to reach nearly one percentage point in 1998, more than offsetting a deceleration in domestic demand. Both private consumption and business fixed investment may lose some buoyancy, but residential investment - which recorded a small decline in 1996 - should recover, spurred by lower interest rates. With output rising above potential and with a somewhat lower effective exchange rate, some inflationary pressures are likely to emerge."

"The major risks and uncertainties concern the reaction of wages and prices to this situation of incipient overheating. The outcome will also depend on external factors, such as the strength of the upturn in continental Europe generally and further exchange rate movements."
